title: Leasable Capacity Windows and Emergency Reclaim - PRD
creator: Asha Patel
description: Problem: Customers require predictable reserved capacity but also need the platform to reclaim short-term spare capacity for bursty workloads. Current reserved pools are static and either overprovisioned or risk underutilization. This PRD defines a leasable-window model plus an emergency reclaim mechanism that lets Redwood offer temporary, revocable capacity while preserving tenant SLAs and predictable billing.
goals: Allow tenants to advertise time-bounded 'leases' for reserved capacity that can be subleased for short windows when idle
Provide an emergency reclaim path with configurable grace and compensation rules so critical workloads can be preempted safely
Expose controls in Console and API to set lease policies, reclaim tolerances, and compensatory billing adjustments
Maintain latency and availability SLOs for reserved-tenants under normal and reclaim scenarios
non_goals: Replace existing reservation contracts or billing models (this augments reserved pools)
Allow unbounded preemption without explicit tenant opt-in for reclaimable leases
Implement complex market-based bidding for leases in this phase
requirements: R1: Lease window creation API - tenants can create a lease that marks a subset of their reserved pool as reclaimable for a time range (start, end, reclaimable_after).
R2: Lease heartbeat - an SDK/agent heartbeat must run (TTL configurable) to keep a lease active; missed heartbeats trigger graceful reclaim sequence.
R3: Console UI - lease editor with visual timeline, current utilization, and estimated reclaimed capacity metrics.
R4: Emergency reclaim policy - platform can mark leases for reclaim based on priority, zone pressure, or manual operator action; reclaim triggers notifications and a configurable grace period.
R5: Graceful eviction paths - support tenant-configurable fallback model variants, reduced concurrency, and ordered request draining during reclaim.
R6: Billing adjustment - when a lease is reclaimed early, the system calculates compensatory credit or prorated refund and surfaces it on the invoice.
R7: Observability - per-lease metrics (utilization, reclaim events, time to drain) and audit logs for actions and operator overrides.
R8: Access control - RBAC rules restrict who can create/modify leases; audit logs emit actor and justification.
R9: Backwards compatibility - existing reserved pools continue to function unchanged unless tenant opts into leasing feature.
R10: Canary rollout flags to enable server-side behavior for a subset of customers for initial validation.
acceptance_criteria: AC1: API - createLease endpoint accepts lease payload and returns lease id; a subsequent GET returns identical lease parameters.
AC2: Heartbeat - when heartbeat is sent at configured TTL, lease remains active; missing heartbeat triggers 'reclaim_pending' state within configured reclaimable_after + grace window.

AC3: Reclaim flow - platform-initiated reclaim moves workload to 'draining' state, respects tenant fallback policy (if set) and finishes within configured max_grace_seconds; requests beyond that are preempted.
AC4: Billing - a reclaimed lease results in a line-item credit equal to the unused portion of the lease commitment; credit calculation matches billing team formula (unit tests provided).
AC5: Metrics - Console shows per-lease utilization and a timeline for at least 90% of leases created during test period; reclaim events are queryable via the audit API.
AC6: RBAC - only users with 'lease:manage' permission can create/modify leases; attempts by others return HTTP 403.
AC7: Backfill safety - when reclaimed capacity is used by other tenants, the system never allows total reserved capacity consumption to exceed zone capacity (simulated test).
AC8: Performance - enabling leases for a tenant adds <5% p95 latency overhead to non-reclaimed requests in steady-state.
AC9: Rollout - feature flags and canary control allow enabling for 5% of tenants, with monitoring alerts firing on unexpected reclaim failure rates (>2% reclaim ops failing per hour).
scope_changes: Scope originally included market-style bidding; removed to keep MVP focused on deterministic lease windows and operator-driven reclaim.
Initial plan had automated cross-zone evacuation; deferred to future phase to limit blast radius.
Added heartbeat requirement after engineering review to reduce silent lease drift and improve reclaim confidence.
tradeoffs: Choosing time-bounded leases simplifies billing and reasoning but requires tenants to predict usage; alternative dynamic leasing adds complexity.
Implementing heartbeat increases reliability of reclaim but requires tenants to run an agent or integrate SDK; this may limit early adoption.
Grace periods improve tenant experience but increase risk of reclaim failure under sudden capacity pressure. We choose configurable grace to balance.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (canary): implement API + internal operator UI, enable for Redwood-run test tenants (1-2 tenants).
Phase 2 (pilot): enable for selected pilot customers via feature flag with Console UI and billing credits visible; monitor reclaim reliability and billing correctness.
Phase 3 (GA): broad enablement with full Console controls, RBAC, and public docs; migration tooling for tenants to opt-in to leaseable subsets.
Rollback: feature flag toggle to disable new reclaim flows; system must show no lingering 'draining' leases after rollback within 24h.
metrics: Percent of reclaimed leases that drain within grace window (target >= 98%)
Billing credit accuracy (discrepancies <0.1% in sample audits)
P95 latency delta for non-reclaimed requests post-enablement (<5% increase)
Number of tenant complaints / high-severity incidents related to reclaim (target 0 in pilot)
risks_mitigations: Risk: Silent tenant workloads lost due to missed heartbeat - Mitigation: require explicit opt-in and provide SDK + dashboard showing heartbeat health.
Risk: Billing disputes after early reclaim - Mitigation: transparent invoice line items and provisional credits; customer support playbook drafted.
Risk: Operator-initiated reclaim causes cascading failures - Mitigation: rate-limit reclaim ops, circuit-breaker for zone-level reclaim, and preflight simulation tool.
Risk: Complexity overload for small tenants - Mitigation: offer simple default lease profile and a one-click Console toggle for managed leases.
dependencies_and_notes: Depends on autoscaling improvements from ENG-1842 (kernel-level queue backpressure) for reliable draining.
Billing team to review credit formula and provide unit conversion table (action: schedule meeting by 2025-02-20).
Design: add a compact lease timeline widget; initial mockups linked in Drive: https://drive.example.com/leasenav (placeholder).
Security: confirm RBAC scope and audit log retention (security review not required for MVP but recommended before GA).
notes: Implementation approach suggested by infra team: maintain a per-lease state machine (active, reclaim_pending, draining, reclaimed, expired).
Operator UX should include a 'simulate reclaim' button for debugging and dry-run validation with metrics emitted to the console dashboard.
We will ship a public API contract doc and example client snippets for Go/Python/Node as part of the pilot.
Acceptance test plan to include chaos scenario: sudden zone pressure while leases are draining to validate safety guards.
